statement: For real numbers $a, b \ge 0$ and [Hölder conjugate exponents](c:holder-conjugate-exponents) $p, q > 1$ with $1/p + 1/q = 1$, $ab \le a^p/p + b^q/q$, with equality if and only if $a^p = b^q$.

hypotheses.text: The numbers $a$ and $b$ are nonnegative reals.
The exponents satisfy $p, q > 1$ and $1/p + 1/q = 1$, so they are [Hölder conjugate](c:holder-conjugate-exponents).

conclusion: $ab \le a^p/p + b^q/q$, and equality holds exactly when $a^p = b^q$.

formal.difference: The declaration states the inequality for extended nonnegative reals, where a or b may be infinite, and omits the equality case. The equality case is the separate declaration Real.young_inequality_eq_iff_of_nonneg.

proofs.name: Weighted AM-GM
proofs.slogan: Apply the weighted AM-GM inequality to $a^p$ and $b^q$ with the weights $1/p$ and $1/q$.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem for finite $a, b \ge 0$, including $a = 0$ or $b = 0$. The extended-real case of the declaration adds only the trivial case $a = \infty$ or $b = \infty$.

roles.why: Nonnegative bases make the real powers defined and give $(a^p)^{1/p} = a$.
Conjugacy turns $1/p$ and $1/q$ into weights with sum one.

steps.slogan: Check that $1/p$ and $1/q$ are positive weights with sum one.
steps.detail: Because $p, q > 1$, the numbers $1/p$ and $1/q$ lie in $(0, 1)$. The conjugacy relation $1/p + 1/q = 1$ makes them the weights of a [weighted mean](c:weighted-mean).

steps.slogan: Apply the two-term weighted AM-GM inequality to $x = a^p$ and $y = b^q$.
steps.detail: For weights $w_1 + w_2 = 1$ and $x, y \ge 0$, weighted AM-GM gives $x^{w_1} y^{w_2} \le w_1 x + w_2 y$. With $x = a^p$, $y = b^q$, $w_1 = 1/p$ and $w_2 = 1/q$, the right side is $a^p/p + b^q/q$.

steps.slogan: Simplify the geometric mean $(a^p)^{1/p} (b^q)^{1/q}$ to the product $ab$.
steps.detail: For $a, b \ge 0$ the power rule gives $(a^p)^{1/p} = a$ and $(b^q)^{1/q} = b$. So the left side of step 2 is $ab$, and the inequality follows.

steps.slogan: Characterize equality by the strict convexity of the [exponential function](c:exponential-function).
steps.detail: For $a, b > 0$ write $a^p = e^s$, $b^q = e^t$; then $ab = e^{s/p + t/q} \le e^s/p + e^t/q$, with equality only if $s = t$ because $\exp$ is [strictly convex](c:strictly-convex-function). If $a = 0$ or $b = 0$, equality forces both to vanish. Conversely $a^p = b^q = c$ gives $ab = c = c/p + c/q$.

concepts.c:holder-conjugate-exponents: The conjugate exponents give the two weights of the mean.
concepts.c:weighted-mean: Young's inequality is a two-term weighted mean inequality.
concepts.c:exponential-function: Writing powers as exponentials exposes the convexity behind equality.
concepts.c:strictly-convex-function: Strict convexity of the exponential forces equal points at equality.

source.note: mathlib reduces to NNReal.young_inequality_real and Real.young_inequality_of_nonneg, which apply geom_mean_le_arith_mean2_weighted; equality uses geom_mean_eq_arith_mean2_weighted_iff_of_nonneg.

proofs.name: Area under a power curve
proofs.slogan: Cover the rectangle $[0, a] \times [0, b]$ by the region under $y = x^{p-1}$ and the region left of the same curve.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem for $a, b \ge 0$. If $a = 0$ or $b = 0$ the rectangle has area zero and the argument still applies.

roles.why: Nonnegative $a$ and $b$ give a rectangle in the first quadrant, where the curve lives.
Conjugacy makes $y^{q-1}$ the inverse of $x^{p-1}$ and gives $(p - 1)q = p$.

steps.slogan: Define the increasing function $f(x) = x^{p-1}$ and its inverse $g(y) = y^{q-1}$.
steps.detail: Conjugacy gives $(p - 1)(q - 1) = 1$, so $g(f(x)) = x$ for $x \ge 0$ and $g$ is the [inverse function](c:inverse-function) of $f$. Both functions are continuous and strictly increasing on $[0, \infty)$ with value $0$ at $0$.

steps.slogan: Compute the two areas $\int_0^a f = a^p/p$ and $\int_0^b g = b^q/q$.
steps.detail: The power rule gives $\int_0^a x^{p-1}\,dx = a^p/p$ and $\int_0^b y^{q-1}\,dy = b^q/q$. The first [integral](c:riemann-integral) is the area under the graph over $[0, a]$; the second is the area between the graph and the $y$-axis for $0 \le y \le b$.

steps.slogan: Show that the two regions together cover the rectangle $[0, a] \times [0, b]$.
steps.detail: A point $(x, y)$ of the rectangle with $y \le f(x)$ lies under the graph, and a point with $y > f(x)$ has $x < g(y)$, so it lies left of the graph. The regions overlap only on the graph, which has area zero, so $ab \le a^p/p + b^q/q$.

steps.slogan: Show that the excess area vanishes exactly when $b = a^{p-1}$.
steps.detail: If $b < f(a)$, the region under the graph has a part of positive area above the rectangle; if $b > f(a)$, the other region sticks out to the right. Equality $b = a^{p-1}$ is equivalent to $b^q = a^{(p-1)q} = a^p$.

concepts.c:holder-conjugate-exponents: Conjugate exponents make the two power curves inverse to each other.
concepts.c:inverse-function: The second region is the area under the inverse function.
concepts.c:riemann-integral: The two areas are computed as integrals of power functions.

source.note: The classical area argument of W. H. Young (1912), as in Hardy, Littlewood and Pólya, Inequalities (1934).

statement: For finitely many reals $z_i \ge 0$ and weights $w_i \ge 0$ with $\sum_i w_i = 1$, the weighted geometric mean is at most the [weighted arithmetic mean](c:weighted-mean): $\prod_i z_i^{w_i} \le \sum_i w_i z_i$. Equal weights give $\sqrt[n]{z_1 \cdots z_n} \le (z_1 + \dots + z_n)/n$.

hypotheses.text: Every weight satisfies $w_i \ge 0$.
The weights have sum one: $\sum_i w_i = 1$, so they define a [weighted mean](c:weighted-mean).
Every value satisfies $z_i \ge 0$.

formal.difference: The declaration states the weighted form over a finite index set. The equal-weight form is the substitution w_i = 1/n.

proofs.name: Jensen for the exponential
proofs.slogan: Write each positive $z_i$ as $e^{\log z_i}$ and apply Jensen's inequality to the convex exponential function.
proofs.scope: Two cases: some $z_i = 0$ has positive weight, or every $z_i$ with positive weight is positive. Terms with $w_i = 0$ contribute $z_i^0 = 1$ to the product and $0$ to the sum, with $0^0 = 1$.

roles.why: Nonnegative weights keep the sum nonnegative in the zero case and are needed for Jensen's inequality.
Weights with sum one form a convex combination, which Jensen's inequality requires.
Nonnegative values make the real powers defined and the right side nonnegative.

steps.slogan: Settle the case where some zero value $z_i$ has positive weight.
steps.detail: If $z_i = 0$ and $w_i > 0$, then $z_i^{w_i} = 0$, so the product is $0$. The sum $\sum_j w_j z_j$ is nonnegative because all weights and values are nonnegative.

steps.slogan: Write the product as the exponential $\exp(\sum_i w_i \log z_i)$.
steps.detail: Drop the indices with $w_i = 0$; they contribute $1$ to the product and $0$ to the sum. In the case left after step 1, every remaining $z_i$ is positive, so $z_i^{w_i} = e^{w_i \log z_i}$ with the [logarithm](c:logarithm) defined.

steps.slogan: Apply Jensen's inequality to the convex exponential at the points $\log z_i$.
steps.detail: The [exponential function](c:exponential-function) is [convex](c:convex-function), and the weights are nonnegative with sum one. Jensen's inequality gives $\exp(\sum_i w_i \log z_i) \le \sum_i w_i e^{\log z_i} = \sum_i w_i z_i$.

steps.slogan: Combine the two cases into the inequality for all nonnegative values.
steps.detail: Step 1 covers a weighted zero, and steps 2 and 3 give $\prod_i z_i^{w_i} \le \sum_i w_i z_i$ when every weighted value is positive. The two cases exhaust all possibilities.

concepts.c:weighted-mean: The right side is the weighted arithmetic mean that bounds the product.
concepts.c:logarithm: Logarithms turn the weighted product into a weighted sum.
concepts.c:exponential-function: The exponential undoes the logarithm and carries the convexity.
concepts.c:convex-function: Convexity of the exponential is the inequality's real content.

source.note: mathlib splits off a weighted zero (Finset.prod_eq_zero) and applies ConvexOn.map_sum_le to convexOn_exp at the points log z_i.

proofs.name: Pólya's tangent-line bound
proofs.slogan: Bound each ratio $z_i/A$ by $e^{z_i/A - 1}$, where $A$ is the arithmetic mean, and multiply the weighted bounds.
proofs.scope: The case $A = \sum_i w_i z_i > 0$. If $A = 0$, every $z_i$ with $w_i > 0$ is zero, and some $w_i > 0$ exists, so both sides are $0$.

roles.why: Nonnegative exponents $w_i$ keep each inequality when both sides are raised to the power $w_i$.
The weight sum one makes the exponent vanish and turns $A^{\sum w_i}$ into $A$.
Nonnegative values make the ratios $z_i/A$ nonnegative, so their real powers are defined.

steps.slogan: Prove the tangent-line bound $x \le e^{x - 1}$ for every real $x$.
steps.detail: The function $h(x) = e^{x-1} - x$ has $h'(x) = e^{x-1} - 1$, which is negative for $x < 1$ and positive for $x > 1$. So $h$ has its minimum $h(1) = 0$; this is the tangent line of the convex [exponential function](c:exponential-function) at $x = 1$.

steps.slogan: Divide by the arithmetic mean $A = \sum_i w_i z_i$ and bound each ratio $z_i/A$.
steps.detail: For $A > 0$, step 1 gives $0 \le z_i/A \le e^{z_i/A - 1}$. Raising both sides to the power $w_i \ge 0$ keeps the order: $(z_i/A)^{w_i} \le e^{w_i(z_i/A - 1)}$.

steps.slogan: Multiply the weighted bounds and evaluate the exponent with the weight sum.
steps.detail: The product of the right sides is $\exp(\sum_i w_i z_i/A - \sum_i w_i) = e^{1 - 1} = 1$. The product of the left sides is $\prod_i z_i^{w_i}/A^{\sum_i w_i} = \prod_i z_i^{w_i}/A$, so $\prod_i z_i^{w_i} \le A$, the [weighted mean](c:weighted-mean).

concepts.c:weighted-mean: The arithmetic mean $A$ normalizes the values and is the bound.
concepts.c:exponential-function: The bound $x \le e^{x-1}$ turns the product into an exponential of a sum.

source.note: G. Pólya's proof by the bound $x \le e^{x-1}$, as in J. M. Steele, The Cauchy-Schwarz Master Class (2004), chapter 2.

statement: For every [set](c:set) $A$, no function $f\colon A \to \mathcal{P}(A)$ into the [power set](c:power-set) is a [surjection](c:surjection). Hence $|A| < |\mathcal{P}(A)|$.

hypotheses.text: The map $f\colon A \to \mathcal{P}(A)$ is any function from a [set](c:set) $A$ to its power set.

conclusion: Some subset of $A$ is not a value of $f$, and $|A| < |\mathcal{P}(A)|$.

formal.difference: The declaration proves only that no map from a type to its power set is surjective. The strict cardinal inequality is the separate declaration Cardinal.cantor.

proofs.name: Diagonal set
proofs.slogan: Form the set of points that are not in their own image and show that no point maps onto it.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem, including $A = \emptyset$, where the empty map misses $\emptyset \in \mathcal{P}(A)$.

roles.why: The map is arbitrary, so the diagonal set defeats every candidate surjection.

steps.slogan: Define the diagonal set $D = \{a \in A : a \notin f(a)\}$.
steps.detail: The set $D$ is a [subset](c:subset) of $A$, so $D \in \mathcal{P}(A)$. Membership of $a$ in $D$ is the negation of membership of $a$ in $f(a)$.

steps.slogan: Assume that $D = f(d)$ for some $d$ and derive a contradiction.
steps.detail: If $f(d) = D$, then $d \in D$ holds if and only if $d \notin f(d) = D$. A statement equivalent to its own negation is false, so no such $d$ exists and $f$ is not a [surjection](c:surjection).

steps.slogan: Embed $A$ into $\mathcal{P}(A)$ by the singleton map $a \mapsto \{a\}$.
steps.detail: Distinct points have distinct singletons, so this map is an [injection](c:injection). Hence $|A| \le |\mathcal{P}(A)|$.

steps.slogan: Combine the injection and the missing surjection into $|A| < |\mathcal{P}(A)|$.
steps.detail: Equal [cardinal numbers](c:cardinal-number) would give a bijection $A \to \mathcal{P}(A)$, which is a surjection. Step 2 excludes this, so the inequality of step 3 is strict.

concepts.c:set: The argument works for every set, finite or infinite.
concepts.c:power-set: The diagonal set is an element of the power set.
concepts.c:surjection: The theorem denies the existence of a surjection onto the power set.
concepts.c:subset: The diagonal set is a subset built from the map itself.
concepts.c:injection: The singleton injection gives the non-strict inequality.
concepts.c:cardinal-number: The conclusion compares the cardinal numbers of the two sets.

source.note: mathlib takes a preimage of {a | a ∉ f a} and derives the contradiction with iff_not_self; Cardinal.cantor gives the strict inequality.

statement: If a point $x$ lies in the [convex hull](c:convex-hull) of a set $P \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$, then $x$ is a convex combination of at most $d + 1$ [affinely independent](c:affine-independence) points of $P$. So $x$ lies in a [simplex](c:simplex) with vertices in $P$.

hypotheses.text: The point $x$ lies in the [convex hull](c:convex-hull) of a set $P \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$.

conclusion: There are affinely independent points $p_1, \dots, p_m \in P$ with $m \le d + 1$ and $x$ in their convex hull.

formal.difference: The declaration writes the convex hull as the union of the hulls of affinely independent finite subsets, over any linearly ordered field and any vector space. The bound m ≤ d + 1 then follows because an affinely independent set in R^d has at most d + 1 points.

proofs.name: Minimal representation
proofs.slogan: Take a representation of $x$ with the fewest points and show that an affine dependence would give a shorter one.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem. The hypothesis excludes $P = \emptyset$, whose hull is empty.

roles.why: Membership in the hull supplies a first finite convex combination.

steps.slogan: Write $x$ as a convex combination of finitely many points of $P$.
steps.detail: The [convex hull](c:convex-hull) of $P$ is the set of finite sums $\sum_i \lambda_i p_i$ with $p_i \in P$, $\lambda_i \ge 0$ and $\sum_i \lambda_i = 1$. So $x$ has such a representation.

steps.slogan: Choose a representation $x = \sum_{i=1}^m \lambda_i p_i$ with the fewest points.
steps.detail: The number of points is a positive integer, so a least one exists. Minimality forces every $\lambda_i > 0$, because a point with weight zero could be dropped.

steps.slogan: Suppose that the points are affinely dependent and choose a nonzero relation among them.
steps.detail: [Affine independence](c:affine-independence) fails exactly when some $\mu \ne 0$ has $\sum_i \mu_i p_i = 0$ and $\sum_i \mu_i = 0$. Because the $\mu_i$ sum to zero and are not all zero, some $\mu_i$ is positive.

steps.slogan: Shift the weights along the relation until one weight reaches zero.
steps.detail: Let $t = \min\{\lambda_i/\mu_i : \mu_i > 0\}$ and $\lambda_i' = \lambda_i - t\mu_i$. Then $\lambda_i' \ge 0$, $\sum_i \lambda_i' = 1$, $\sum_i \lambda_i' p_i = x$ and some $\lambda_j' = 0$, which gives a shorter representation against minimality.

steps.slogan: Bound the number of affinely independent points in $\mathbb{R}^d$ by $d + 1$.
steps.detail: If $m \ge d + 2$, the linear map $\mu \mapsto (\sum_i \mu_i p_i, \sum_i \mu_i)$ from $\mathbb{R}^m$ to $\mathbb{R}^{d+1}$ has a nonzero kernel by rank-nullity, an affine dependence. So the minimal points are affinely independent, $m \le d + 1$, and they span a [simplex](c:simplex) that contains $x$.

concepts.c:convex-hull: The hull is the set of finite convex combinations of points of $P$.
concepts.c:affine-independence: An affine dependence is exactly what lets the proof drop a point.
concepts.c:simplex: Affinely independent points span a simplex that contains $x$.

source.note: mathlib picks a minimal-cardinality finset (Caratheodory.minCardFinsetOfMemConvexHull) and drops a point of an affinely dependent set (Caratheodory.mem_convexHull_erase).

statement: In the untyped [lambda calculus](c:lambda-calculus), [beta-reduction](c:beta-reduction) is [confluent](c:confluence): if $M \twoheadrightarrow_\beta N_1$ and $M \twoheadrightarrow_\beta N_2$, then some term $P$ satisfies $N_1 \twoheadrightarrow_\beta P$ and $N_2 \twoheadrightarrow_\beta P$.

hypotheses.text: The term $M$ reduces to $N_1$ in zero or more [beta-reduction](c:beta-reduction) steps.
The term $M$ reduces to $N_2$ in zero or more beta-reduction steps.

conclusion: Some term $P$ satisfies $N_1 \twoheadrightarrow_\beta P$ and $N_2 \twoheadrightarrow_\beta P$.

formal.difference: The declaration proves confluence of word reduction in free additive groups, a different rewriting system, not of beta-reduction. Its proof has the same shape: a one-step diamond property and the tiling lemma Relation.church_rosser.

proofs.name: Parallel reduction
proofs.slogan: Contract many redexes at once, prove the diamond property for this parallel reduction, and tile the diamonds over reduction sequences.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem, with terms taken up to renaming of bound variables. Zero-step reductions are included, so $N_1 = M$ or $N_2 = M$ is covered.

roles.why: The first reduction sequence gives one side of the grid of diamonds.
The second reduction sequence gives the other side of the grid.

steps.slogan: Define parallel reduction $\Rightarrow$, which contracts any chosen set of redexes in one step.
steps.detail: The rules are $x \Rightarrow x$; $M \Rightarrow M'$ gives $\lambda x.M \Rightarrow \lambda x.M'$; and $M \Rightarrow M'$, $N \Rightarrow N'$ give $MN \Rightarrow M'N'$ and $(\lambda x.M)N \Rightarrow M'[x := N']$. This [reduction](c:reduction) may contract nested redexes together.

steps.slogan: Show that one beta step is a parallel step and a parallel step is a beta sequence.
steps.detail: Induction on terms and on the rules gives $\to_\beta \subseteq \Rightarrow \subseteq \twoheadrightarrow_\beta$. Hence the reflexive-transitive closure of $\Rightarrow$ equals $\twoheadrightarrow_\beta$, the closure of [beta-reduction](c:beta-reduction).

steps.slogan: Prove that parallel reduction is compatible with substitution.
steps.detail: If $M \Rightarrow M'$ and $N \Rightarrow N'$, then $M[x := N] \Rightarrow M'[x := N']$. The proof is an induction on the derivation of $M \Rightarrow M'$, with the substitution lemma in the redex case.

steps.slogan: Prove the diamond property of $\Rightarrow$ with the complete development $M^*$.
steps.detail: Let $M^*$ contract every redex of $M$ at once. Induction on the derivation of $M \Rightarrow N$, with step 3 in the redex case, gives $N \Rightarrow M^*$, so any two parallel steps from $M$ meet at $M^*$.

steps.slogan: Tile the one-step diamonds to join two parallel reduction sequences.
steps.detail: Induction on the lengths of the two sequences fills a grid with the diamonds of step 4; its far corner $P$ is reachable from $N_1$ and from $N_2$. By step 2 these sequences are beta reductions, so beta-reduction is [confluent](c:confluence).

concepts.c:lambda-calculus: The terms and the redexes are those of the untyped lambda calculus.
concepts.c:beta-reduction: Beta-reduction is the relation whose confluence the theorem asserts.
concepts.c:confluence: Confluence is the joinability that the tiling produces.
concepts.c:reduction: Parallel reduction is an auxiliary relation with the same closure.

source.note: The Tait and Martin-Löf proof with Takahashi's complete development, as in H. P. Barendregt, The Lambda Calculus: Its Syntax and Semantics, chapter 3. The tiling step is the argument of mathlib's Relation.church_rosser.

statement: Let $(X_n)_{n \ge 0}$ be a supermartingale for a [filtration](c:filtration) $(\mathcal{F}_n)$ with $\sup_n \mathbb{E}|X_n| < \infty$. Then $X_n$ converges [almost surely](c:almost-sure-convergence) to an integrable limit $X_\infty$. If $(X_n)$ is also [uniformly integrable](c:uniform-integrability), then $X_n \to X_\infty$ in $L^1$. The same holds for submartingales and [martingales](c:martingale).

hypotheses.text: The process $(X_n)$ is adapted and integrable, with [conditional expectations](c:conditional-expectation) $\mathbb{E}[X_{n+1} \mid \mathcal{F}_n] \le X_n$.
The process is bounded in $L^1$: $\sup_n \mathbb{E}|X_n| < \infty$.
For the $L^1$ statement, the family $(X_n)$ is [uniformly integrable](c:uniform-integrability).

conclusion: $X_n \to X_\infty$ almost surely with $\mathbb{E}|X_\infty| < \infty$, and also in $L^1$ under uniform integrability.

proofs.name: Upcrossings
proofs.slogan: Bound the expected number of upcrossings of each rational interval, exclude oscillation, and pass to the limit with Fatou's lemma.
proofs.scope: Supermartingales; a submartingale $X$ follows by applying the proof to $-X$. Steps 1 to 4 give almost sure convergence, and step 5 adds $L^1$ convergence under uniform integrability.

roles.why: The supermartingale property makes the upcrossing strategy lose money on average.
The $L^1$ bound makes the upcrossing bound and the Fatou bound finite.
Uniform integrability turns almost sure convergence into $L^1$ convergence.

steps.slogan: Bound the expected upcrossings of $[a, b]$ by Doob's upcrossing inequality.
steps.detail: Let $U_N[a, b]$ count the upcrossings of $[a, b]$ by $X_0, \dots, X_N$. Betting on each upcrossing is a predictable strategy, so the supermartingale property gives $(b - a)\,\mathbb{E}\,U_N[a, b] \le \mathbb{E}(X_N - a)^- \le \sup_n \mathbb{E}|X_n| + |a|$.

steps.slogan: Let $N \to \infty$ to show that each interval has finitely many upcrossings almost surely.
steps.detail: By monotone convergence, $U_\infty[a, b] = \lim_N U_N[a, b]$ has $\mathbb{E}\,U_\infty[a, b] \le (\sup_n \mathbb{E}|X_n| + |a|)/(b - a) < \infty$. So $U_\infty[a, b] < \infty$ almost surely.

steps.slogan: Exclude oscillation by a countable union over rational pairs $a < b$.
steps.detail: If the [limit inferior](c:limit-inferior) of $X_n$ is below its limit superior, some rational pair $a < b$ lies between them and $X$ crosses $[a, b]$ infinitely often. A countable union of null events is null, so $X_n$ converges almost surely to some $X_\infty \in [-\infty, \infty]$.

steps.slogan: Apply Fatou's lemma to show that the limit is finite and integrable.
steps.detail: Fatou's lemma gives $\mathbb{E}|X_\infty| \le \liminf_n \mathbb{E}|X_n| \le \sup_n \mathbb{E}|X_n| < \infty$. So $X_\infty$ is an [integrable function](c:integrable-function) and is finite almost surely.

steps.slogan: Upgrade the almost sure convergence to $L^1$ convergence by uniform integrability.
steps.detail: A uniformly integrable sequence that converges almost surely converges in $L^1$ by the Vitali convergence theorem. So $\mathbb{E}|X_n - X_\infty| \to 0$ when $(X_n)$ is uniformly integrable.

concepts.c:filtration: The filtration defines predictable betting strategies on upcrossings.
concepts.c:almost-sure-convergence: Almost sure convergence is the first conclusion of the theorem.
concepts.c:uniform-integrability: Uniform integrability is the extra hypothesis for $L^1$ convergence.
concepts.c:martingale: Martingales are supermartingales, so they are covered by the proof.
concepts.c:conditional-expectation: The supermartingale inequality is stated with conditional expectations.
concepts.c:limit-inferior: Convergence means that the limit inferior equals the limit superior.
concepts.c:integrable-function: Fatou's lemma shows that the limit is integrable.

source.note: Doob's upcrossing proof, as in D. Williams, Probability with Martingales (1991), chapters 11 and 13.

statement: There is a constant $p_{\mathrm{th}} > 0$ such that, if each location of a noisy [quantum circuit](c:quantum-circuit) fails independently with probability $p < p_{\mathrm{th}}$, every ideal circuit with $T$ locations can be simulated with error at most $\varepsilon$ by a noisy circuit with $O(T\,\mathrm{polylog}(T/\varepsilon))$ locations.

hypotheses.text: Each location (gate, preparation, measurement or wait) fails independently with probability at most $p$.
The fault rate is below the threshold: $p < p_{\mathrm{th}}$.

conclusion: The noisy circuit reproduces the output distribution of the ideal circuit up to error $\varepsilon$, with polylogarithmic overhead.

proofs.name: Concatenated distance-3 codes
proofs.slogan: Encode recursively in a distance-3 code so that each level squares the effective failure rate, then choose the number of levels.
proofs.scope: An outline of the published proof for independent stochastic noise. The gadget constructions and the count of malignant fault pairs rest on the cited work.

roles.why: Independent faults make the probability of two faults in one rectangle at most $A p^2$.
A rate below $1/A$ makes the iterated bound decay doubly exponentially.

steps.slogan: Replace each location by a fault-tolerant gadget on a distance-3 code.
steps.detail: Each logical [qubit](c:qbit) is encoded in a distance-3 [error correcting code](c:error-correcting-code) such as Steane's 7-qubit code. Each gate becomes an encoded gate followed by error correction, and the cited work builds these gadgets so that one fault in an extended rectangle leaves a correctable error.

steps.slogan: Bound the failure probability of one extended rectangle by counting fault pairs.
steps.detail: An extended rectangle fails only if it contains at least two faults. With at most $A$ pairs of locations in a rectangle, a union bound gives failure probability at most $A p^2$.

steps.slogan: Concatenate the code $k$ times and iterate the bound level by level.
steps.detail: In the [concatenated code](c:concatenated-code), a level-$k$ rectangle acts like a level-$(k-1)$ location with failure rate $p_k \le A p_{k-1}^2$. Hence $p_k \le (A p)^{2^k}/A$, which decays doubly exponentially when $p < p_{\mathrm{th}} = 1/A$.

steps.slogan: Choose the number $k$ of levels so that the total failure probability is at most $\varepsilon$.
steps.detail: A union bound over the $T$ simulated locations needs $T p_k \le \varepsilon$, so $k = O(\log\log(T/\varepsilon))$ levels suffice. Each level multiplies the size by a constant, so the overhead is $\mathrm{polylog}(T/\varepsilon)$.

concepts.c:quantum-circuit: The theorem simulates an ideal quantum circuit by a noisy one.
concepts.c:qbit: Each logical qubit is stored in many physical qubits.
concepts.c:error-correcting-code: A distance-3 code corrects any single fault in a gadget.
concepts.c:concatenated-code: Concatenation squares the failure rate at each level.

source.ref: P. Aliferis, D. Gottesman and J. Preskill, Quantum accuracy threshold for concatenated distance-3 codes, Quantum Information and Computation 6 (2006), 97-165
source.note: Earlier threshold proofs are due to Aharonov and Ben-Or, Knill, Laflamme and Zurek, and Kitaev (1996-1997).

statement: Let $A(t)$ be a continuous $n \times n$ matrix function with period $T > 0$. Then every [fundamental matrix](c:fundamental-matrix) of the [linear ODE](c:linear-ode) $x' = A(t)x$ has the form $\Phi(t) = P(t)e^{tB}$, where $P$ is continuously differentiable, invertible and $T$-periodic and $B$ is a constant complex matrix.

hypotheses.text: The coefficient matrix $A\colon \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{C}^{n \times n}$ is continuous.
The coefficients are [periodic](c:periodic-coefficients): $A(t + T) = A(t)$ for all $t$, with $T > 0$.
$\Phi$ is a [fundamental matrix](c:fundamental-matrix): its columns are $n$ linearly independent solutions of $x' = A(t)x$.

conclusion: $\Phi(t) = P(t)e^{tB}$ with $P(t + T) = P(t)$ invertible for all $t$ and $B$ constant.

proofs.name: Monodromy matrix and its logarithm
proofs.slogan: Show that the shifted fundamental matrix is the original times a constant monodromy matrix, take a logarithm of it, and define $P$ by division.
proofs.scope: The complex form of the theorem. For real $A$ the same steps with a real logarithm of $M^2$ give a real $P$ of period $2T$.

roles.why: Continuity of $A$ gives existence and uniqueness of solutions of the linear system.
Periodicity makes the shifted matrix solve the same equation.
Invertibility of $\Phi$ makes the monodromy matrix invertible, so it has a logarithm.

steps.slogan: Show that the shifted matrix $\Psi(t) = \Phi(t + T)$ is again a fundamental matrix.
steps.detail: Periodicity gives $\Psi'(t) = A(t + T)\Phi(t + T) = A(t)\Psi(t)$. The matrix $\Psi(t)$ is invertible because $\Phi(t + T)$ is, so $\Psi$ is a [fundamental matrix](c:fundamental-matrix).

steps.slogan: Show that $\Phi(t + T) = \Phi(t)M$ for the constant matrix $M = \Phi(0)^{-1}\Phi(T)$.
steps.detail: Both $\Phi(t + T)$ and $\Phi(t)M$ solve $X' = A(t)X$ with the value $\Phi(T)$ at $t = 0$. Uniqueness for the linear initial value problem gives equality for all $t$, and $M$ is the invertible [monodromy](c:monodromy) matrix.

steps.slogan: Take a [matrix logarithm](c:matrix-logarithm) $B$ with $e^{TB} = M$.
steps.detail: Every invertible complex matrix has a logarithm: on a Jordan block $\lambda(I + N)$ with $\lambda \ne 0$ and $N$ nilpotent, use $(\log\lambda)I + \sum_{k \ge 1} (-1)^{k+1}N^k/k$, a finite sum. Set $B = T^{-1}\log M$.

steps.slogan: Define $P(t) = \Phi(t)e^{-tB}$ and check that $P$ has period $T$.
steps.detail: $P$ is invertible and continuously differentiable as a product of such matrices, with the [matrix exponential](c:matrix-exponential) $e^{-tB}$. Steps 2 and 3 give $P(t + T) = \Phi(t)Me^{-TB}e^{-tB} = P(t)$, so $P$ is a [periodic function](c:periodic-function) and $\Phi(t) = P(t)e^{tB}$.

concepts.c:fundamental-matrix: The theorem describes the structure of every fundamental matrix.
concepts.c:periodic-coefficients: Periodic coefficients make the time shift a symmetry of the equation.
concepts.c:monodromy: The monodromy matrix records how solutions change over one period.
concepts.c:matrix-logarithm: A logarithm of the monodromy matrix gives the constant matrix $B$.
concepts.c:matrix-exponential: The factor $e^{tB}$ carries the non-periodic part of the solution.
concepts.c:periodic-function: The factor $P$ is the periodic part of the fundamental matrix.

source.note: Floquet's argument (1883), as in E. A. Coddington and N. Levinson, Theory of Ordinary Differential Equations (1955), chapter 3.

statement: In the [linear regression](c:linear-regression) model $y = X\beta + \varepsilon$ with $X$ of full column rank, $\mathbb{E}\varepsilon = 0$ and $\operatorname{Cov}(\varepsilon) = \sigma^2 I$, the [least squares](c:least-squares) estimator $\hat\beta = (X^\top X)^{-1}X^\top y$ has the least [variance](c:variance) among linear [unbiased estimators](c:unbiased-estimator): $\operatorname{Var}(c^\top\tilde\beta) \ge \operatorname{Var}(c^\top\hat\beta)$ for every $c$.

hypotheses.text: The $n \times p$ design matrix $X$ is fixed and has rank $p$.
The errors have mean zero: $\mathbb{E}\varepsilon = 0$.
The errors are uncorrelated with common variance: the [covariance matrix](c:covariance-matrix) is $\operatorname{Cov}(\varepsilon) = \sigma^2 I$.
The competitor $\tilde\beta = Cy$ is linear in $y$ and unbiased: $\mathbb{E}\tilde\beta = \beta$ for every $\beta$.

proofs.name: Decompose the competitor
proofs.slogan: Write the competitor's matrix as the least squares matrix plus a correction $D$ with $DX = 0$, and expand the covariance.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem. If $\sigma^2 = 0$, both covariances vanish and the inequality is an equality.

roles.why: Full rank makes $X^\top X$ invertible, so $\hat\beta$ is defined.
Zero-mean errors give $\mathbb{E}\,Cy = CX\beta$.
Spherical errors give $\operatorname{Cov}(Cy) = \sigma^2 CC^\top$.
Unbiasedness for every $\beta$ forces $CX = I$.

steps.slogan: Show that the least squares estimator is linear and unbiased.
steps.detail: Full rank makes $X^\top X$ invertible, so $\hat\beta = C_0 y$ with $C_0 = (X^\top X)^{-1}X^\top$. Then $\mathbb{E}\hat\beta = C_0 X\beta = \beta$ because $\mathbb{E}\varepsilon = 0$; so it is an [unbiased estimator](c:unbiased-estimator).

steps.slogan: Translate unbiasedness of $\tilde\beta = Cy$ into the matrix equation $CX = I$.
steps.detail: $\mathbb{E}\,Cy = CX\beta$, and this equals $\beta$ for every $\beta$ only if $CX = I$. Write $C = C_0 + D$; because $C_0 X = I$, the correction satisfies $DX = 0$.

steps.slogan: Expand the covariance of $Cy$ and show that the cross terms vanish.
steps.detail: $\operatorname{Cov}(Cy) = C\operatorname{Cov}(\varepsilon)C^\top = \sigma^2(C_0 + D)(C_0 + D)^\top$. The cross term $DC_0^\top = DX(X^\top X)^{-1}$ is $0$, so $\operatorname{Cov}(\tilde\beta) = \operatorname{Cov}(\hat\beta) + \sigma^2 DD^\top$ with $\operatorname{Cov}(\hat\beta) = \sigma^2(X^\top X)^{-1}$.

steps.slogan: Conclude from the identity $c^\top DD^\top c = |D^\top c|^2 \ge 0$.
steps.detail: The matrix $\sigma^2 DD^\top$ is [positive semidefinite](c:positive-semidefinite-matrix). Hence $\operatorname{Var}(c^\top\tilde\beta) - \operatorname{Var}(c^\top\hat\beta) = \sigma^2|D^\top c|^2 \ge 0$ for every $c$.

concepts.c:linear-regression: The model $y = X\beta + \varepsilon$ is the setting of the theorem.
concepts.c:least-squares: The least squares estimator is the claimed best estimator.
concepts.c:variance: The theorem compares variances of linear combinations of estimators.
concepts.c:unbiased-estimator: Unbiasedness restricts the competitors to matrices with $CX = I$.
concepts.c:covariance-matrix: The error covariance $\sigma^2 I$ makes the cross terms vanish.
concepts.c:positive-semidefinite-matrix: The covariance gap $\sigma^2 DD^\top$ is positive semidefinite.

source.note: The standard matrix proof, as in G. A. F. Seber and A. J. Lee, Linear Regression Analysis, 2nd ed. (2003), chapter 3.

statement: Let a [Lie group](c:lie-group) $G$ act linearly on $\mathbb{R}^n$, let $V$ be a smooth $G$-invariant potential, and let $\phi_0$ be a minimum of $V$ with [stabilizer](c:stabilizer) $H$. Then the mass matrix $\partial_i\partial_j V(\phi_0)$ has at least $\dim G - \dim H$ zero eigenvalues: each broken generator gives a massless Goldstone boson.

hypotheses.text: A [Lie group](c:lie-group) $G$ acts linearly on the field space $\mathbb{R}^n$.
The potential $V\colon \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}$ is smooth and $G$-invariant: $V(g\phi) = V(\phi)$.
The vacuum $\phi_0$ is a minimum of $V$ with stabilizer $H$, so the symmetry is [spontaneously broken](c:spontaneously-broken-symmetry) when $H \ne G$.

conclusion: The [Hessian](c:hessian) of $V$ at $\phi_0$ vanishes on the tangent space of the orbit $G\phi_0$, which has dimension $\dim G - \dim H$.

proofs.name: Differentiate the invariance twice
proofs.slogan: Differentiate the invariance of the potential along each generator, then differentiate again at the vacuum, where the gradient vanishes.
proofs.scope: The classical (tree-level) theorem; the same argument applied to the quantum effective potential gives the version of Goldstone, Salam and Weinberg. Only the vanishing gradient at $\phi_0$ is used.

roles.why: The linear action supplies the generators $X$ and the orbit through $\phi_0$.
Invariance gives the identity that the proof differentiates twice.
At the vacuum the gradient vanishes, and its stabilizer fixes the count of broken generators.

steps.slogan: Differentiate $V(e^{sX}\phi) = V(\phi)$ at $s = 0$ for each generator $X$.
steps.detail: For $X$ in the [Lie algebra](c:lie-algebra) $\mathfrak{g}$, acting by a matrix on $\mathbb{R}^n$, invariance gives $\sum_i \partial_i V(\phi)\,(X\phi)_i = 0$ for every $\phi$.

steps.slogan: Differentiate the identity again in $\phi$ and evaluate it at the vacuum.
steps.detail: Differentiation in $\phi_j$ gives $\sum_i \partial_j\partial_i V(\phi)(X\phi)_i + \sum_i \partial_i V(\phi)X_{ij} = 0$. At the minimum $\phi_0$ the gradient vanishes, so $\operatorname{Hess} V(\phi_0)\,X\phi_0 = 0$.

steps.slogan: Count the independent zero modes $X\phi_0$ by rank-nullity.
steps.detail: The linear map $X \mapsto X\phi_0$ on $\mathfrak{g}$ has as kernel the Lie algebra of the [stabilizer](c:stabilizer) $H$. By rank-nullity its image, the tangent space of the [orbit](c:orbit), has dimension $\dim G - \dim H$ and lies in the kernel of the [Hessian](c:hessian).

steps.slogan: Read the zero eigenvalues of the mass matrix as massless particles.
steps.detail: Expanding $V$ to second order around $\phi_0$ gives the mass matrix $\partial_i\partial_j V(\phi_0)$ of the field fluctuations. Step 3 gives at least $\dim G - \dim H$ zero [eigenvalues](c:eigenvalue), one massless Goldstone field for each broken generator.

concepts.c:lie-group: The continuous symmetry group supplies the generators.
concepts.c:stabilizer: The stabilizer's generators are unbroken and give no zero mode.
concepts.c:spontaneously-broken-symmetry: Broken symmetry means $H \ne G$, so the count is positive.
concepts.c:hessian: The Hessian at the vacuum is the mass matrix of the fields.
concepts.c:lie-algebra: Each Lie algebra element gives one infinitesimal invariance identity.
concepts.c:orbit: Moving along the vacuum orbit costs no energy.
concepts.c:eigenvalue: Zero eigenvalues of the mass matrix are massless particles.

source.note: The classical proof, as in M. E. Peskin and D. V. Schroeder, An Introduction to Quantum Field Theory (1995), section 11.1; the quantum version is J. Goldstone, A. Salam and S. Weinberg, Broken symmetries, Phys. Rev. 127 (1962), 965-970.

statement: For every finite alphabet $A$ and every finite number $r$ of colors there is a dimension $N$ such that every coloring of the cube $A^N$ with $r$ colors has a monochromatic [combinatorial line](c:combinatorial-line).

hypotheses.text: The alphabet $A$ is a [finite set](c:finite-set).
The number $r$ of colors is finite.

conclusion: Some dimension $N$ makes every $r$-coloring of $A^N$ contain a combinatorial line whose points all have one color.

proofs.name: Color focusing
proofs.slogan: Induct on the alphabet size, and in the step build more and more color-focused lines until two of them share a color.
proofs.scope: Induction on $|A|$; an empty alphabet makes the claim vacuous. The step from $A$ to $A' = A \cup \{\ast\}$ uses the theorem for $A$ with a much larger number of colors.

roles.why: Finiteness of $A$ allows the induction on its size and keeps the slice colorings finite in number.
Finitely many colors keep the slice colorings finite and bound the number of distinct colors.

steps.slogan: Settle the empty alphabet and set up the step from $A$ to $A' = A \cup \{\ast\}$.
steps.detail: For an empty alphabet there is nothing to color, so the claim holds. The step assumes the theorem for $A$ with every finite number of colors and proves it for $A'$.

steps.slogan: State the key claim: in high dimension there are $k$ color-focused lines or a monochromatic line.
steps.detail: Lines in $A'^N$ are color-focused if they share the point with letter $\ast$, and each line is monochromatic on its points with letters from $A$, in distinct colors. The claim is proved by induction on $k$, and $k = 0$ is trivial.

steps.slogan: Split the coordinates as $\iota \sqcup \iota'$ and color $A^{\iota'}$ by whole slices.
steps.detail: A coloring of $A'^{\iota \sqcup \iota'}$ colors each $v \in A^{\iota'}$ by the induced coloring of its slice $A'^{\iota}$, with at most $r^{|A'|^{|\iota|}}$ colors. The theorem for $A$ gives a [combinatorial line](c:combinatorial-line) $l'$ in $A^{\iota'}$ on which all slices carry the same coloring $C'$.

steps.slogan: Combine $k$ focused lines for $C'$ with the line $l'$ into $k + 1$ focused lines.
steps.detail: By the claim for $k$ in dimension $\iota$, $C'$ has a monochromatic line or $k$ focused lines with focus $f$. If a line has the color of $f$, it is monochromatic; otherwise the products of the $k$ lines with $l'$ and the line through $f$ along $l'$ give $k + 1$ focused lines.

steps.slogan: Take $k = r + 1$ and note that $r + 1$ lines cannot have distinct colors.
steps.detail: Only $r$ colors exist, so by the pigeonhole principle the focused alternative of the claim fails for $k = r + 1$. Hence the claim gives a monochromatic line, which completes the step from $A$ to $A'$.

concepts.c:combinatorial-line: The theorem finds a monochromatic combinatorial line, and the step uses one in $A^{\iota'}$.
concepts.c:finite-set: A finite alphabet allows induction on its number of letters.

source.note: mathlib proves exists_mono_in_high_dimension' by induction on α through Option α, with ColorFocused families of AlmostMono lines and the constructions Line.prod and Line.vertical.

statement: Let $f\colon [0, \infty) \to \mathbb{R}$ be nonnegative and nonincreasing. Then the [series](c:series) $\sum_{n \ge 0} f(n)$ converges if and only if the [improper integral](c:improper-integral) $\int_0^\infty f(x)\,dx$ converges, and then $\int_0^\infty f \le \sum_{n \ge 0} f(n) \le f(0) + \int_0^\infty f$.

hypotheses.text: The function $f$ is nonnegative on $[0, \infty)$.
The function $f$ is nonincreasing, a [monotone function](c:monotone-function) on $[0, \infty)$.

conclusion: The series and the integral converge together, with $\int_0^\infty f \le \sum_{n \ge 0} f(n) \le f(0) + \int_0^\infty f$.

formal.difference: The declaration gives only the upper bound, and it assumes integrability on (0, ∞); summability from integrability is AntitoneOn.summable_of_integrableOn_Ioi_zero. The converse and the lower bound are not part of it.

proofs.name: Squeeze on unit intervals
proofs.slogan: Squeeze the integral over each interval $[n, n + 1]$ between $f(n + 1)$ and $f(n)$ and add the inequalities.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem. The integrals over bounded intervals exist because a monotone function is Riemann integrable.

roles.why: Nonnegativity makes the partial sums and the integrals $\int_0^X f$ increase.
Monotonicity squeezes $f$ on each unit interval between its end values.

steps.slogan: Bound the integral over $[n, n + 1]$ by the values of $f$ at the two ends.
steps.detail: For $x \in [n, n + 1]$, monotonicity gives $f(n + 1) \le f(x) \le f(n)$. A monotone function is [Riemann integrable](c:riemann-integral) there, so $f(n + 1) \le \int_n^{n+1} f \le f(n)$.

steps.slogan: Add the local bounds to compare partial sums with integrals.
steps.detail: Summation over $n < N$ gives $\sum_{n=1}^{N} f(n) \le \int_0^N f \le \sum_{n=0}^{N-1} f(n)$. So the partial sum $S_N = \sum_{n=0}^{N} f(n)$ satisfies $\int_0^{N+1} f \le S_N \le f(0) + \int_0^N f$.

steps.slogan: Show that the partial sums and the integrals $\int_0^X f$ both increase.
steps.detail: Because $f \ge 0$, $S_N$ increases with $N$ and $\int_0^X f$ increases with $X$. A nondecreasing quantity converges exactly when it is bounded above.

steps.slogan: Transfer boundedness between the sums and the integrals and pass to the limit.
steps.detail: By step 2, a bound on the [improper integral](c:improper-integral) bounds every $S_N$, and a bound on the [series](c:series) bounds every $\int_0^{N+1} f$. Step 3 gives convergence of both, and $N \to \infty$ in step 2 gives the two inequalities.

concepts.c:series: The test decides the convergence of the series.
concepts.c:improper-integral: The improper integral is the comparison object for the series.
concepts.c:monotone-function: Monotonicity gives the squeeze on each unit interval.
concepts.c:riemann-integral: Monotone functions are Riemann integrable on bounded intervals.

source.note: mathlib bounds f(n + 1) by the integral over [n, n + 1] (AntitoneOn.sum_le_integral), derives AntitoneOn.tsum_add_one_le_integral and AntitoneOn.summable_of_integrableOn_Ioi_zero, and splits off f(0).

statement: Let $(X_t)_{t \in [a, b]}$ be a centered, square-integrable [stochastic process](c:stochastic-process) with continuous [covariance function](c:covariance-function) $K$. Let $e_k$ be the orthonormal eigenfunctions of the integral operator with kernel $K$, with eigenvalues $\lambda_k > 0$. Then $X_t = \sum_k Z_k e_k(t)$ in mean square, uniformly in $t$, where $Z_k = \int_a^b X_t e_k(t)\,dt$ are uncorrelated with variance $\lambda_k$.

hypotheses.text: The process is centered with finite second moments: $\mathbb{E}X_t = 0$ and $\mathbb{E}X_t^2 < \infty$.
The [covariance function](c:covariance-function) $K(s, t) = \mathbb{E}X_sX_t$ is continuous on $[a, b]^2$.
The $e_k$ form an [orthonormal basis](c:orthonormal-basis) of the closed range of the [integral operator](c:integral-operator) with kernel $K$, with $\int_a^b K(s, t)e_k(t)\,dt = \lambda_k e_k(s)$.

proofs.name: Mercer expansion of the covariance
proofs.slogan: Compute the covariances of the coefficients from the eigenvalue equation, then identify the mean-square error with the tail of Mercer's series.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem; the $Z_k$ are mean-square Riemann integrals, which exist because $K$ is continuous. The eigenvalues are nonnegative because $K$ is positive semidefinite.

roles.why: Mean zero and finite variance make $K$ the covariance and give $\mathbb{E}Z_k = 0$.
Continuity of $K$ is the hypothesis of Mercer's theorem and makes the $Z_k$ well defined.
The eigenvalue equation turns integrals of $K$ against $e_k$ into $\lambda_k e_k$.

steps.slogan: Expand the covariance function by Mercer's theorem.
steps.detail: $K$ is continuous, symmetric and positive semidefinite, so Mercer's theorem gives $K(s, t) = \sum_k \lambda_k e_k(s)e_k(t)$ with absolute and uniform convergence on $[a, b]^2$.

steps.slogan: Compute $\mathbb{E}X_tZ_k$ and $\mathbb{E}Z_jZ_k$ by exchanging expectation and integration.
steps.detail: Fubini's theorem gives $\mathbb{E}X_tZ_k = \int_a^b K(t, s)e_k(s)\,ds = \lambda_k e_k(t)$. Integrating again against $e_j$ gives $\mathbb{E}Z_jZ_k = \lambda_k\delta_{jk}$ by orthonormality, and $\mathbb{E}Z_k = 0$.

steps.slogan: Expand the mean-square error of the partial sum $S_N(t) = \sum_{k \le N} Z_k e_k(t)$.
steps.detail: Step 2 gives $\mathbb{E}(X_t - S_N(t))^2 = K(t, t) - 2\sum_{k \le N}\lambda_k e_k(t)^2 + \sum_{k \le N}\lambda_k e_k(t)^2 = K(t, t) - \sum_{k \le N}\lambda_k e_k(t)^2$.

steps.slogan: Let $N \to \infty$ and use the uniform convergence of Mercer's series on the diagonal.
steps.detail: By step 1 the right side of step 3 tends to $0$ uniformly in $t \in [a, b]$. So $S_N(t) \to X_t$ in mean square, uniformly in $t$, with the uncorrelated coefficients of step 2.

concepts.c:stochastic-process: The theorem expands a whole process in a deterministic basis.
concepts.c:covariance-function: The covariance function is the kernel whose eigenfunctions form the basis.
concepts.c:orthonormal-basis: Orthonormality of the $e_k$ makes the coefficients uncorrelated.
concepts.c:integral-operator: The eigenfunctions come from the integral operator with kernel $K$.

source.note: The classical proof by Mercer's theorem (Karhunen 1946, Loève 1955); see M. Loève, Probability Theory (Van Nostrand, 1955).

statement: Over an alphabet of $D \ge 1$ letters, every finite [uniquely decodable code](c:uniquely-decodable-code) with codeword lengths $\ell_1, \dots, \ell_m$ satisfies $\sum_i D^{-\ell_i} \le 1$. Conversely, if positive integers $\ell_1, \dots, \ell_m$ satisfy this inequality, some [prefix code](c:prefix-code) has exactly these codeword lengths.

hypotheses.text: The alphabet is finite with $D \ge 1$ letters.
For the inequality: the finite code is [uniquely decodable](c:uniquely-decodable-code), so distinct sequences of codewords have distinct concatenations.
For the converse: the positive integers $\ell_1, \dots, \ell_m$ satisfy $\sum_i D^{-\ell_i} \le 1$.

conclusion: Unique decodability gives $\sum_i D^{-\ell_i} \le 1$, and lengths with this property are the lengths of a prefix code.

formal.difference: The declaration proves only the inequality for a finite uniquely decodable code. The converse construction of a prefix code is not part of it.

proofs.name: Power counting and greedy construction
proofs.slogan: Raise the Kraft sum to a high power and count concatenations by length, then build a prefix code greedily for the converse.
proofs.scope: Steps 1 to 3 prove the inequality and steps 4 and 5 the converse with base-$D$ expansions for $D \ge 2$. For $D = 1$ the inequality allows a single length, and one word is a prefix code.

roles.why: The $D$ letters bound the number of words of length $\ell$ by $D^\ell$ and give base-$D$ expansions.
Unique decodability makes distinct tuples of codewords give distinct concatenations.
The inequality keeps each start point $c_i$ below $1$ and separates the intervals of the codewords.

steps.slogan: Expand the $r$-th power of the Kraft sum $K = \sum_w D^{-|w|}$ over $r$-tuples of codewords.
steps.detail: $K^r = \sum_{(w_1, \dots, w_r)} D^{-(|w_1| + \dots + |w_r|)}$, and the exponent is the length of the concatenation $w_1 \cdots w_r$. With $L$ the largest codeword length, this length is at most $rL$.

steps.slogan: Bound the tuples whose concatenation has length $\ell$ by the $D^\ell$ words of that length.
steps.detail: Unique decodability makes the map from tuples to concatenations injective, and there are $D^\ell$ words of length $\ell$. Each length $\ell \le rL$ contributes at most $D^\ell D^{-\ell} = 1$, so $K^r \le rL$.

steps.slogan: Compare the exponential growth of $K^r$ with the linear bound $rL$.
steps.detail: If $K > 1$, then $K^r/(rL) \to \infty$ as $r \to \infty$, which contradicts step 2 for large $r$. Hence $K \le 1$.

steps.slogan: Sort the lengths and give word $i$ the first $\ell_i$ digits of $c_i = \sum_{j < i} D^{-\ell_j}$.
steps.detail: Sort $\ell_1 \le \dots \le \ell_m$. The hypothesis gives $c_i \le 1 - D^{-\ell_i} < 1$, and $c_i$ is a multiple of $D^{-\ell_i}$, so its base-$D$ expansion has at most $\ell_i$ digits; let $w_i$ be these $\ell_i$ digits.

steps.slogan: Check that no word $w_i$ is a prefix of a later word $w_k$.
steps.detail: For $i < k$, $c_k \ge c_i + D^{-\ell_i}$, so $c_k$ lies outside the interval $[c_i, c_i + D^{-\ell_i})$ of numbers whose expansion starts with $w_i$. Hence the words are distinct and form a [prefix code](c:prefix-code) with the given lengths.

steps.slogan: Join the inequality of steps 1 to 3 with the construction of steps 4 and 5.
steps.detail: Steps 1 to 3 prove the inequality for every uniquely decodable code, and steps 4 and 5 realize every admissible length list by a prefix code. Together they give both parts of the theorem.

concepts.c:uniquely-decodable-code: Unique decodability makes the count of concatenations injective.
concepts.c:prefix-code: The converse constructs a prefix code from admissible lengths.

source.note: mathlib bounds K^r by r times the largest length (kraft_mcmillan_inequality_aux) and lets r grow (tendsto_self_mul_const_pow_of_abs_lt_one); the converse steps are authored, after Kraft (1949).

statement: Let $T$ be a [complete](c:complete-statistic) [sufficient statistic](c:sufficient-statistic) for a family $\{P_\theta\}$. If $\delta(T)$ is an [unbiased estimator](c:unbiased-estimator) of $g(\theta)$ with finite variance, then $\delta(T)$ has the least [variance](c:variance) among all unbiased estimators of $g(\theta)$ for every $\theta$, and it is the only such estimator up to almost sure equality.

hypotheses.text: The statistic $T$ is [sufficient](c:sufficient-statistic) for $\theta$.
The statistic $T$ is [complete](c:complete-statistic): $\mathbb{E}_\theta h(T) = 0$ for all $\theta$ implies $h(T) = 0$ almost surely.
The estimator $\delta(T)$ depends on the data only through $T$, is unbiased for $g(\theta)$ and has finite variance.

conclusion: $\delta(T)$ is the unique uniformly minimum-variance unbiased estimator of $g(\theta)$.

proofs.name: Rao-Blackwell and completeness
proofs.slogan: Improve any unbiased estimator by conditioning on $T$, and use completeness to show that the improvement is always $\delta(T)$.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem; competitors with infinite variance need no argument. Uniqueness holds almost surely under every $P_\theta$.

roles.why: Sufficiency makes $\mathbb{E}[W \mid T]$ a statistic that does not depend on $\theta$.
Completeness forces two unbiased functions of $T$ to agree.
Unbiasedness of $\delta(T)$ gives $\mathbb{E}_\theta(\varphi - \delta)(T) = 0$ for every $\theta$.

steps.slogan: Condition an arbitrary unbiased estimator $W$ on $T$ to get $\varphi(T) = \mathbb{E}[W \mid T]$.
steps.detail: Sufficiency makes the [conditional expectation](c:conditional-expectation) $\mathbb{E}_\theta[W \mid T]$ free of $\theta$, so $\varphi(T)$ is a statistic. The tower property gives $\mathbb{E}_\theta\varphi(T) = \mathbb{E}_\theta W = g(\theta)$.

steps.slogan: Bound the variance of $\varphi(T)$ by the variance of $W$.
steps.detail: The conditional variance formula gives $\operatorname{Var}_\theta W = \operatorname{Var}_\theta\varphi(T) + \mathbb{E}_\theta\operatorname{Var}_\theta(W \mid T)$. So $\operatorname{Var}_\theta\varphi(T) \le \operatorname{Var}_\theta W$, with equality only if $W = \varphi(T)$ almost surely.

steps.slogan: Show that $\varphi(T) = \delta(T)$ almost surely by completeness.
steps.detail: The function $h = \varphi - \delta$ has $\mathbb{E}_\theta h(T) = g(\theta) - g(\theta) = 0$ for every $\theta$. [Completeness](c:complete-statistic) gives $h(T) = 0$ almost surely, so $\varphi(T) = \delta(T)$.

steps.slogan: Conclude minimality and uniqueness of $\delta(T)$ from steps 2 and 3.
steps.detail: Steps 2 and 3 give $\operatorname{Var}_\theta\delta(T) \le \operatorname{Var}_\theta W$ for every $\theta$ and every unbiased $W$. If $W$ also has least variance, equality holds in step 2, so $W = \varphi(T) = \delta(T)$ almost surely.

concepts.c:complete-statistic: Completeness makes the unbiased function of $T$ unique.
concepts.c:sufficient-statistic: Sufficiency makes conditioning on $T$ produce a statistic.
concepts.c:unbiased-estimator: The theorem compares all unbiased estimators of $g(\theta)$.
concepts.c:variance: Variance is the risk that the optimal estimator minimizes.
concepts.c:conditional-expectation: Conditioning on $T$ is the Rao-Blackwell improvement.

source.note: The standard proof from the Rao-Blackwell theorem, as in E. L. Lehmann and G. Casella, Theory of Point Estimation, 2nd ed. (1998), chapter 2.
